data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's core undecidability claim asserts that 'genuine reasoning' and 'mere compliance' make identical point predictions for aggregate accuracy, rendering them inseparable. But this collapses a crucial distinction: genuine reasoning generalizes to cases outside the checklist's explicit coverage. A single evaluation can include a held-out probe set of novel cases outside the checklist's scope; if the panel's accuracy on these probe cases significantly exceeds the pure baseline expected from blind checklist compliance (which would predict near-chance or systematic failure on novel cases), genuine reasoning is demonstrated. Thus, the hypotheses do not make identical point predictions across a properly partitioned evaluation set.
